title: Provable Quantization with Randomized Hadamard Transform
claim: A continuous CDF-like map turns equal-width, shifted grid cells in quantile space into non-uniform input buckets with reconstruction points.
layout: single panel, bottom-to-top y-axis, dashed projection lines from quantile grid to buckets
description: A single annotated plot. The x-axis is the input coordinate t and the y-axis is quantile space F(t). A thick blue sigmoid curve F(t) rises from h_0 at the bottom to h_B at the top. A green bell-shaped curve f(t), proportional to F'(t), is centered on a dotted vertical line at t=0. On the y-axis, grid boundaries h_0 to h_B are spaced 1/B apart. Curly braces mark the end cells as (1+U)/B and (1-U)/B, which shows the shift from the dither U. Gray dotted lines run from each h_j to the curve and then down to the x-axis. They split the axis into buckets B_0 to B_3, labeled with braces below. Red dashed lines run from the midpoints m_j to red dots on the curve, then down to the reconstruction points q_j on the x-axis. The eye goes first to the blue S-curve and the red dots.
caption: Illustration of the scalar quantizer mapping with B = 4. The function F(t) (blue) and its scaled underlying density f(t) (green) are shown. A uniform grid shifted by U defines boundaries hj on the y-axis, which project back to the boundaries of the quantization buckets Bj. The reconstruction values qj are defined as the inverse image of the bucket midpoints mj = (hj + hj+1)/2.
abstract: Vector quantization via random projection followed by scalar quantization is a fundamental primitive in machine learning, with applications ranging from similarity search to federated learning and KV cache compression. While dense random rotations yield clean theoretical guarantees, they require $\Theta(d^2)$ time. The randomized Hadamard transform $HD$ reduces this cost to $O(d \log d)$, but its discrete structure complicates analysis and leads to weaker or purely empirical compression guarantees. In this work, we introduce DASHQuant (**D**ithered **A**ccelerated **S**ingle-**H**adamard **Quant**ization) a provable variant of this approach. Specifically, the quantizer applies $HD$ to the input vector and adds a random dithering before quantizing, injecting additional randomness at negligible cost. We prove that this approach is unbiased and provides mean squared error bounds that asymptotically match those achievable with truly random rotation matrices. In particular, we prove that a dithered version of TurboQuant, and a special case of EDEN, achieves mean squared error $\bigl(\pi\sqrt{3}/2 + o(1)\bigr) \cdot 4^{-b}$ at $b$ bits per coordinate, where the $o(1)$ term vanishes uniformly over all unit vectors and all dimensions as the number of quantization levels grows.
